sourceRestrictions:
# Frozen source restrictions — Debate 289

The canonical source is the complete supplied 2020 Wielenberg–Johnson recording, video bg2WK-IIrd8. This is not the 2018 Craig–Wielenberg event. The publisher dates it September 27, 2020, University of Nebraska-Lincoln. The motion is byte-identically: What is the best account of objective morality?

Pro: Adam Lloyd Johnson — God grounds objective morality. Con: Erik Wielenberg — Objective morality needs no divine foundation. Both accept objective morality. Assess their comparative explanations and actual challenges; do not require either to prove objective morality against a nihilist, or require Wielenberg to disprove every God merely because he offers a non-theistic moral account.

## Approved scope

This assessment covers only the debaters’ direct exchange (approximately 33:05–1:13:25), as approved by the editor. The introductory position discussion, audience questions and all dependent answers, including the final reply to an audience question, are excluded. This recording has no separate formal opening speeches or paired closing statements. Neither speaker receives credit, penalties, or an inference of failing to reply from excluded material. These scores assess the direct exchange, not the complete recording.

The chapter starts at about 33:05; Wielenberg’s first substantive direct question begins at 33:22 (canonical index 916, human label E0917). Retained argument ends at 1:13:25.840 (canonical index 2006, E2007). Index 2007 is “My time is up,” and index 2008 starts the audience transition. Exclude all earlier and later source from ratings, quotations, responses, burdens and absence inferences. Earlier propositions restated independently in the retained exchange may be assessed only in that retained form; do not import excluded reasons. A shared assumption can identify the debate’s issue without receiving evidential credit.

Read the full source to establish boundaries. Moderator interjections only assign turns or time. No substantive host argument belongs to a scored side. No opening or closing should be invented from this dialogue. Do not treat Johnson’s final answer after the audience animal-value question as a formal closing.

## Event indexing and ownership

The indexed transcript uses human labels E0001 through E3103. The events array and every startEvent/endEvent field are ZERO-BASED: E0001 corresponds to index 0; subtract one from each human label. Millisecond endpoints come from events.json exactly. Caption display durations overlap turn transitions; they do not establish overlapping speech. Choose the smallest complete supporting text and avoid mixed handoff events.

Direct-exchange ownership (human E labels, inclusive):
- Wielenberg question E0917–E0977; Johnson answer E0978–E1055.
- Johnson question E1058–E1072; Wielenberg answer E1073–E1184.
- Wielenberg question E1188–E1235; exclude mixed E1236; Johnson answer E1237–E1321.

- Johnson question E1552–E1606, with its last summary clause spilling into mixed E1607; exclude E1607. Earlier full supporting challenge remains available. Wielenberg answer E1608–E1712.
- Wielenberg question E1716–E1738; Johnson answer E1739–E1825.
- Johnson question E1829–E1898; Wielenberg answer E1899–E2007.
Other material inside the window is logistical. Do not claim finer audio verification than available.

## Automatic-caption limitations

Only one English track exists; no alternative English transcript was available. Initial public audio byte probe returned 206, but full public retrieval returned 403, so no audio was acquired and no paid transcription occurred. The seven planned clip checks were NOT completed. No direct audio listening is claimed. Every selected below-high-attribution move still needs successful required verification before adjudication; never label uncertainty high merely to avoid that requirement.

Do not derive a rating or quotation from: E1718’s uncertain transition polarity; E1748’s “communitarian” label (the theory is repeatedly called Trinitarian elsewhere); E1894’s corrupt first animal name (“beanies”); mixed handoffs E1236 and E1607. Do not silently correct them. Clear surrounding arguments may be assessed without these terms. Outside-scope caption names such as “William Lane Craig” addressing Wielenberg are recognition errors, not another participant or scored error. General disfluency or caption syntax is not evidence of poor reasoning.

## Complete featured quotations

Every eligible quote must be an exact, self-contained complete thought, 3–18 words, retaining any qualification necessary to represent the speaker fairly. Do not truncate a concession before a challenge. Examples of complete clear candidates within the assessed source are Johnson’s “the ultimate good is what God is like.” (E1055), and Wielenberg’s “a mother's love for her child is intrinsically good.” (E1623–E1624). The inventory author must verify any chosen quote in its selected exact source span and surrounding context before freeze; these examples do not prescribe move selection or ratings.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: God himself, rather than an ungrounded moral proposition, is the ultimate stopping point.
moves.warrant: Facts about God's triune loving character describe the ultimate being; humans call that character good and discover it as the ultimate good.
moves.inference: The account grounds moral truth in a concrete supreme being rather than free-standing axioms.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers Johnson's complete answer from his explicit disagreement through the distinction between God and facts about God, then his direct account of why Trinitarian love is called good. The length is required because both the ontological stopping point and the goodness challenge must be answered together.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Yeah, and this would be an area where we disagree. So, I think um a theistic explanation, at least a in my Trinitarian moral theory, doesn't have any uh ungrounded moral truths. And so, I I do uh affirm that my theory uh grounds all moral truth in God. And so, um this this moral axiom that he's uh saying in my theory is ungrounded, I wouldn't see it that way. It doesn't seem to me to be an ungrounded uh moral truth. So, according to my theory, the you know, the Trinitarian moral theory that I've proposed, it's that God himself is the the ultimate stopping point that has no further explanation. And I affirm there has to be some sort of an ultimate stopping point in reality. I mean, that's that's part and parcel of their Aristotelian first cause argument that there's got to be some ultimate stopping point. And so, I'm affirming that that is God, the supreme being, and it's he himself that is the the ultimate ultimate stopping point. And then certainly there are facts about God, right? So, I'm I'm affirming that God is, let's say, infinite, um that he exists as three divine persons. Uh I'm affirming, or at least part of my theory, is that he exists in these three loving relationships between Father, Son, and Spirit uh Holy Spirit, so he's triune. So, certainly there are facts uh about God, but it's not that the facts themselves are ultimate. The the facts are just describing who and what God is, but it's God himself is what is what is ultimate. So, um more pertinent to his question, though, what makes their loving relationships good? This is how I would explain that. I would say, um you know, before anything else was created, before anything else existed, you know, there there was just God, right? So, he's the ultimate stopping point, according to my theory. So, God exists as these three divine persons in loving relationship with one another. And they have certain um if you will, ways that they treat each other. So, they're they're kind to one another, they uh respect each other, they care for each other, they want what's best for each other, they're they're unselfish uh towards one another, and that's just how they treat one another. And you can refer to that however you want. And then, you know, as humans, as we come along later, as I would understand it, he created us uh human persons, we're persons, not divine persons, we human persons, and we refer to the way that God is um by just calling that good. And uh maybe we learn that, maybe we learn what is moral good from our interactions, but then we discover that the ultimate good is what God is like.

moves.description: Johnson makes God, rather than propositions about God, the ultimate reality and identifies God’s triune loving character as what humans recognize and call good.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson offers a clear ontological distinction between God as the concrete ultimate reality and propositions that merely describe God, thereby giving his grounding account a definite terminus rather than leaving it at an unexplained sentence or abstract rule. Principal limitation: Listing divine kindness, respect, care, and unselfishness does not explain why those traits are morally good; saying humans call them good risks relabeling the target property instead of grounding it, so Wielenberg’s specific challenge remains only partly answered. Live burden: Johnson must supply a non-circular bridge from God’s character to its normative value and show why a concrete bearer explains goodness better than Wielenberg’s fundamental moral truths.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: A theistic account also appears to rely on an unexplained moral axiom: that Trinitarian love is good.
moves.warrant: If that goodness has no further explanation, theism and non-theistic realism both ultimately appeal to foundational moral truths.
moves.inference: The alleged explanatory advantage of grounding everything in God is reduced.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's complete statement that his own view has foundational moral axioms, continues through his claim that any objective-morality theory likely contains them, and ends with his complete question about what makes Trinitarian love good.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator gives Wielenberg the first direct question, he addresses Adam by name, and the uninterrupted question continues through E0977.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This attacks the claimed difference between divine grounding and Wielenberg's fundamental moral axioms.

burdenContact.rationale: If theism also terminates in a moral axiom, a non-theistic stopping point loses a central comparative disadvantage.

And this might be one of the things Adam and I disagree about. Is that right? And if not, then what would explain the goodness of the love between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. So, not the love itself, but what makes that love good?

moves.description: Wielenberg argues that calling Trinitarian love good may itself be a foundational moral axiom, so divine grounding does not automatically improve on non-theistic moral foundations.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg isolates the precise comparison the motion requires by distinguishing the loving relation from the further proposition that this relation is good, then arguing that an unexplained goodness claim would leave theism and non-theistic realism with structurally similar foundations. Principal limitation: The parity result depends on showing that Johnson cannot ground goodness in God’s concrete character, and this opening challenge poses that question rather than independently demonstrating that every divine-character account must contain an ungrounded moral axiom. Live burden: Johnson must explain why the ultimate being’s loving traits possess moral value without merely redescribing them as kind, caring, respectful, and unselfish, while Wielenberg retains responsibility for defending the claimed symmetry.

moves.description: Johnson compares ultimate stopping points and demands positive reasons for Wielenberg’s basic moral axioms, contrasting their asserted fundamentality with arguments offered for God.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson correctly insists that identifying a proposition as fundamental does not establish its truth and frames a comparative question about which proposed stopping point has stronger reasons and explanatory support. Principal limitation: He names teleological and cosmological arguments without developing them inside the assessed exchange, so the claimed evidential advantage for God is only sketched, while describing Wielenberg’s axioms as merely proposed understates the abductive defense Wielenberg offers. Live burden: Wielenberg must give affirmative grounds for positing necessary moral truths, but Johnson still bears the parallel burden of showing that his cited arguments support the particular triune, morally perfect ground his account requires.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Given Wielenberg's disputed premise that theistic accounts also contain moral axioms, accepting objective morality commits either account to some fundamental moral axioms.
moves.warrant: Objective morality appears real, inference to the best explanation favors basic axioms, and Wielenberg argues that every objective-morality theory—including Johnson's, if his earlier critique is right—contains them.
moves.inference: Conditionally, if Johnson's theory cannot avoid moral axioms, the choice is not God versus brute axioms but objective morality with axioms versus abandoning objective morality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Preserves both parts of Wielenberg's answer: inference to the best explanation and his explicit E1429–E1436 qualification that the argument depends on the unresolved dispute over whether Johnson's account contains axioms.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson's question ends at E1376; Wielenberg answers uninterrupted from E1377 through E1436.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies Wielenberg's positive and explicitly conditional defense of foundational axioms.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends axioms as an unavoidable stopping point only if the same commitment is present in the rival theistic theory.

responseComponents.description: Offers abductive support for axioms while making the equal-footing argument conditional on the disputed theistic-axiom premise.

moves.description: Wielenberg argues abductively for basic moral axioms and conditionally claims that, if theistic morality also contains them, objective morality leaves both accounts on equal footing.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg gives a route from the apparent reality of objective morality to basic axioms and, crucially, states that the parity argument depends on the unresolved premise that Johnson’s theory also contains foundational moral claims. Principal limitation: Invoking inference to the best explanation supplies little comparison among candidate explanations, and the dilemma between accepting axioms and abandoning objectivity works only if that disputed premise succeeds rather than repeated assertion. Live burden: Wielenberg must show why basic truths explain objective morality better than rival grounds and establish the conditional parity premise; Johnson can resist the conclusion by completing his account of divine goodness rather than disproving moral realism.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Abstract moral objects are poor stopping points because they cry out for an explanation.
moves.warrant: Traditions that posit abstract truths have often sought a theistic source, and arguments infer God from such objects.
moves.inference: God offers a deeper explanation than unexplained Platonic entities.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Johnson's question whether Wielenberg still needs Platonic abstract objects and his argument that such objects call for explanation, ending after the completed claim that God is their best explanation and before the redundant unfinished summary that spills into mixed E1607.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator gives Adam the next question; Johnson speaks continuously through E1606, with mixed E1607 excluded.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that apparently abstract moral truths point beyond themselves toward a divine source.

moves.description: Johnson argues that abstract moral entities are inadequate stopping points because they require explanation, and he suggests a divine source offers the deeper account they need.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson presses a legitimate explanatory question about why apparently abstract moral truths should be treated as ultimate and asks whether Wielenberg’s moral realism depends on the controversial ontology of separate Platonic entities. Principal limitation: The move slides among moral truths, brute facts, properties, and abstract objects, relies on undeveloped historical references, and infers that God is probably their source without explaining why a divine mind is a better terminus than the entities themselves. Live burden: Johnson must first establish that Platonism is essential to Wielenberg’s account and then supply the inference from explanatory need to God; Wielenberg may answer the narrower objection by separating concrete property-bearers from optional abstract universals.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: The account needs concrete things with objective moral features but need not require separate abstract objects.
moves.warrant: A mother's love can be intrinsically good whether or not a disputed ontology of abstract properties is correct.
moves.inference: Rejecting Platonic entities does not remove fundamental rightness, wrongness, goodness, and badness.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's complete statement of the philosophical dispute over abstract objects, preserves the concrete-property distinction and his willingness to abandon Platonism, and ends when he completes the claim that particular things retain unsourced moral features. The extended explanation is necessary because the answer separates optional abstract entities from the essential moral properties.

moves.description: Wielenberg separates concrete things bearing moral properties from optional abstract universals, arguing that intrinsic goodness survives regardless of how the independent Platonism dispute is resolved.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg directly undercuts Johnson’s chosen target by distinguishing concrete bearers of moral features from separate abstract property entities and candidly allowing that his moral realism can abandon Platonism if the independent universals debate goes against it. Principal limitation: Removing abstract objects does not explain why concrete relations possess unsourced moral properties, and the bottle and number analogies clarify the ontological distinction without providing new warrant for the mother’s love being intrinsically good. Live burden: Wielenberg must still defend fundamental moral features in concrete reality, but Johnson cannot treat an optional abstract-object ontology as a necessary defect or infer God merely from its explanatory demands.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Okay. So, um Eric, one of the ways that you describe your theory is that it's non-natural. And I was just going to have you, if you would, kind of unpack that and explain what you mean by um that it's that it's non-natural. moves.description: Johnson asks Wielenberg to define non-natural moral properties and address the concern that their departure from physicalism makes the account controversial among atheists.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson asks two diagnostic questions that force Wielenberg to specify what kind of reality moral properties occupy and to acknowledge that atheism alone does not entail acceptance of his non-natural ontology. Principal limitation: Resistance from physicalist atheists is sociological pressure rather than evidence that non-natural moral properties are false, and the challenge supplies no argument establishing either physicalism or the breadth and force of that constituency objection. Live burden: Wielenberg must explain the positive content of non-naturalness and why irreducible moral properties are preferable to physical reduction, while Johnson would need a truth-relevant objection rather than mere discomfort to turn clarification into a comparative advantage.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Objective moral features are real but are not physical features discoverable by empirical science.
moves.warrant: Wrongness appears categorically different from mass or volume; moral reality seems real while resisting physical reduction.
moves.inference: A non-natural moral category is more plausible than either denying morality or reducing it to physics.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's explicit rejection of materialism and scientism, preserves his distinction between science and scientism, explains why moral features are not physical, and includes his answer that physicalist atheists reject the view. The extended span is needed to retain both requested parts and the inference from apparently real but nonphysical morality.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how objective moral reality can be fundamental without being physical or divine.

responseComponents.description: Defines non-natural moral features and accepts, while answering, the objection from physicalist atheists.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I'm not a materialist. I'm not a physicalist. I'm not a I reject this scientist approach. Um not science, but scientism rather. So, I think there's more to reality. I think there's more to the universe than just physical stuff. I think there's more to reality than what can be studied or known through the methods of empirical science. And in particular, if you think about right and wrong and good and evil, on the face of it those seem to be things that aren't really physical features of reality. So, if you think about the water bottle thrilling example I mentioned before, it's got various physical properties, a mass, volume, and so on, other boring physical properties. And then you think about you know, an action for the example I mentioned before, torturing a baby just for fun, and we suppose that that action has this feature or aspect to it, it's it's wrong, it's immoral. It shouldn't be done. And it's really hard to see how that feature could be just a physical feature. It seems to be in a different fundamental category. And so, when I characterize my view as non-natural, basically what I'm saying is that these moral ethical features of things are not part of the natural physical world that can be studied empirically using the methods of science. Um so, the other question was, yeah, does this lead some atheists to not accept my theory? The answer is yes. Those atheists are misguided. They're in the grip of scientism. They accept physicalism. The thing about atheism though, it's very unorganized, Okay, we don't have an official sort of doctrine that we have to adhere to. There's of course within Christianity various debates and disagreements, but atheism is is much more sort of out of control. And it's like the wild west. So it doesn't particularly bother me that this particular type of atheism, this scientist physicalist version, doesn't fit very well with my view of reality. You asked what I would what I would say to those atheists in in that camp. I mean there's a this is a sort of big debate, but there's kind of two things that lead me to this non-natural view. I mentioned before some of the reasons that lead me to think that objective morality is real. And then I just don't see any plausible explanation as to how it could be that right and wrong, good and evil are literally physical features of things. So they seem real, they seem not to be physical, so they must be something else, their own fundamental category. That's what I mean when I call my view non-natural.

moves.description: Wielenberg defines moral properties as real yet nonphysical, reasoning that wrongness differs categorically from measurable features and therefore belongs to a fundamental non-natural domain.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg directly defines non-naturalism, carefully separates science from scientism, and explains through the contrast between wrongness and properties such as mass or volume why objective morality may be real without being physically measurable. Principal limitation: The argument moves largely from moral appearance and the asserted implausibility of physical reduction to a separate fundamental category, without testing sophisticated reductionist alternatives or showing that failure of present empirical access establishes irreducibility. Live burden: Wielenberg must strengthen the inference from apparently nonphysical moral features to genuinely fundamental properties, whereas Johnson cannot defeat the account merely by noting that physicalist atheists reject it.

moves.inference: The hypothetical does not establish intrinsic goodness independently of God.

moves.description: Johnson grants the Godless hypothetical for argument and says evolutionary selection would explain motherly love as survival-enhancing subjective feeling rather than independent objective value.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson eventually accepts Wielenberg’s counterfactual for argument and offers an evolutionary mechanism explaining why caregivers with loving dispositions would protect offspring, survive, and reproduce more successfully than indifferent alternatives. Principal limitation: A causal account of how loving feelings or behavior arose does not show that the resulting relationship lacks objective value, so the reply conflates the origin of a disposition with the truth or ground of a moral property and never excludes their compatibility. Live burden: Johnson must provide the missing inference from evolutionary selection to subjectivity or explain why divine creation uniquely confers value; Wielenberg need not produce a complete alternative worldview merely because he identifies that gap.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Johnson accepts that goodness and obligation are distinct, illustrates the difference with a good but non-obligatory orphanage project, and argues that loving obedience grounds obligation in divine value.
moves.warrant: Moral theories must explain both value and duty; God is the exemplar of goodness, Trinitarian love supplies the value standard, and obedience is intertwined with loving God.
moves.inference: Johnson's account aims to connect obligation to value through loving resemblance, though his stated endpoint specifically explains why obedience is good.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Johnson's complete account that ethical theories must explain both moral value and moral obligation, retains his orphanage illustration of their difference, and continues through his claim that loving obedience resembles Trinitarian love. The length is required to preserve both the accepted distinction and his proposed bridge.

moves.description: Johnson accepts that goodness and duty differ, illustrates supererogatory goodness with an orphanage, then links good obedience to loving God and resembling Trinitarian love.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson explicitly accepts Wielenberg’s value-duty distinction and illustrates it effectively with a morally good orphanage project that is not obligatory, showing that he understands the precise conceptual problem his theory must solve. Principal limitation: His proposed endpoint again establishes that obedience is good because it resembles and expresses divine love, but it never identifies what makes that good act required, effectively restating the premise Wielenberg had already shown insufficient for mustness. Live burden: Johnson must add a principle connecting created persons, divine relationship, or authority to binding duty without assuming the obligation under explanation; Wielenberg need only sustain the exposed gap.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg

moves.warrant: Obligation has a mustness or requirement that goodness by itself does not appear to contain.
moves.inference: Johnson must identify what converts good obedience into a requirement.

moves.description: Wielenberg distinguishes moral value from obligatory mustness and argues that showing obedience resembles divine goodness does not explain why obedience is required.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg identifies the missing inference in Johnson’s account: resemblance to a good exemplar may explain why obedience is valuable, but goodness alone does not entail the mustness that constitutes obligation. Principal limitation: Because the move is a diagnostic challenge, it does not itself provide Wielenberg’s rival theory of obligation or prove that no personal relationship could generate duties, although neither task is required for the objection to succeed. Live burden: Johnson must identify what converts loving resemblance into a binding requirement, while Wielenberg’s narrower burden is to maintain the conceptual distinction rather than establish an entire non-theistic moral system within this question.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Obligations arise because God created humans to love God and others; divine judgment adds accountability but is not presented as the sole generator of duty.

moves.inference: Personal purpose grounds obligation and divine authority accounts for accountability.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers Johnson's answer that created purpose and loving relations generate obligation, then his distinct claim that God as judge adds accountability and punishment. It ends when that judgment point is complete, omitting the following trailing fragment and later salvation detail.

moves.importanceRationale: This states Johnson's personal grounding of duty and distinguishes it from God's enforcement role.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds obligation in God's purpose for persons and accountability in God's authority as judge.

responseComponents.description: Denies that punishment alone generates obligation, locating duty in created loving purpose while retaining divine accountability.

moves.description: Johnson says created loving purpose generates human obligations, while God’s role as moral judge supplies accountability and punishment rather than serving as duty’s sole source.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson answers directly by distinguishing one reading on which God’s creative purpose for humans to love God and others grounds duty from the separate claim that God judges people and supplies accountability for violations. Principal limitation: The response largely asserts that being created for a purpose generates binding duties and does not explain why a creator’s intention has normative authority over persons, leaving the transition from intended function to moral mustness underwarranted. Live burden: Johnson must defend that authority bridge without collapsing obligation into obedience or enforcement, while Wielenberg would need further argument to show that created relational purpose could never contribute to duty.

moves.description: Wielenberg quotes Johnson’s link between guilt and personal authority, then asks whether punishment or getting in trouble is necessary for a moral obligation to exist.

moves.inference: Wielenberg needs a non-theistic account of reliable moral knowledge.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Johnson's complete lucky-coincidence objection: independent moral truths, unguided evolutionary belief formation, possible alternative paths, and the resulting reliability challenge.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator identifies Adam's final question; Johnson presents it uninterrupted from E1829 through E1898.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the principal epistemic challenge to Wielenberg's non-theistic realism.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that theism explains moral-belief reliability while unguided evolution appears not to.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So, um one of the major objections to your theory and um theories like yours is referred to as the lucky coincidence objection. So, let me um let me set this up a little bit here. And this is an objection that um many different folks have proposed against theories like Wielenberg's, not just theists, but atheists have proposed this objection to his theory. And it is often referred to as the lucky coincidence objection. So, here's how it goes. Let me set up the objection and then I want to give, you know, Eric the opportunity to respond to this objection to his theory. So, the objection goes like this. Um basically it says, "Look, if there are such moral objective moral truths uh that exist out there somehow uh in a non-theistic way. So, not saying that God is the ground of them, but they're but they're out there in some way, shape, or form uh beyond naturalism, beyond the, you know, physical world because as he said, he's not a naturalist. So, these non-natural facts, if they do exist out there, how is it that we've come to uh know them? Right? Um if they exist objectively, how did we come about? Especially and this is um you know, a problem that goes back a long ways in philosophy when we posit people have posited these platonic truths out there, how can we know them? But I think this is exacerbated or this problem is amplified for a position like Wielenberg's when uh he affirms that our moral beliefs have come about through a haphazard evolutionary process. So, it seems like quite a lucky coincidence if our you know, moral beliefs have come about in his theory from this haphazard evolutionary process to somehow luckily match up with the objective moral truth that he's proposing. Cuz, for example, you know, even like Charles Darwin said himself, if our evolutionary path would have gone differently, we would have ended up with vastly different moral beliefs, maybe like a beanies or wolves. And so then, how is it that we got so lucky? Our evolutionary path led us to believe these so-called objective moral truths that exist out there.

moves.description: Johnson argues that unguided evolutionary contingency could have produced very different moral beliefs, leaving their alignment with independent necessary moral truths in need of explanation.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson identifies a genuine epistemic challenge by separating independently existing moral truths from beliefs shaped by unguided evolution and asking what explains enough correspondence for humans to possess reliable moral knowledge. Principal limitation: The objection characterizes evolution as haphazard and invokes divergent possible paths only generally, without considering directional selection, cultural correction, or reasoning mechanisms that might reduce the alleged coincidence, so its evidential force remains suggestive rather than measured. Live burden: Wielenberg must explain truth-tracking rather than merely the usefulness of moral beliefs, while Johnson must show that theism actually predicts reliable access rather than simply announcing divine guidance as an available explanation.
moves.sectionTitle: Evolution and access to moral truth

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Moral-belief alignment is imperfect, but necessary moral truths plus partly directional evolutionary pressures and ordinary generalization can explain the degree of alignment that exists.
moves.warrant: The axioms could not have differed; human beliefs vary through evolution, culture, and experience; survival favors recognizing one's own pain and rights, while a useful similarity-based inference extends comparable status to others.
moves.inference: With these qualifications, unguided evolution can move thinkers toward some moral truths without the degree of luck alleged by the objection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's short answer, preserves his concession that beliefs do not align perfectly, his nature-and-nurture qualifications, and the complete two-stage mechanism through E2007. The long span is necessary because omitting any of those qualifications would overstate the proposed evolutionary reliability account.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson's final question ends at E1898; Wielenberg answers continuously from E1899 through the last substantive event E2007.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Wielenberg's complete answer to the central epistemic objection against his account.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains limited moral knowledge through fixed truths, selected self-regarding beliefs, and generalization rather than divine guidance.

responseComponents.description: Concedes imperfect correspondence and offers a qualified evolutionary and inferential mechanism for the alignment that remains.

And now you're off and headed in the direction of moral truth.

moves.description: Wielenberg concedes imperfect alignment, fixes necessary truths on one side, and explains partial convergence through selected self-concern plus similarity-based generalization to others.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg acknowledges imperfect moral agreement and theism’s explanatory advantage, then supplies a two-stage mechanism in which survival favors recognizing one’s own pain and rights while similarity reasoning extends status to others. Principal limitation: The necessity of moral truths removes variation on the truth side but does not make beliefs track them, and although he says recognizing others’ pain and rights is probable and that the process heads toward truth, his claim that generalization inevitably identifies relevant similarity remains too confident. Live burden: Wielenberg must show that selection and reasoning yield truth-sensitive reliability beyond self-protection, while Johnson must not treat every imperfect or natural process as incapable of knowledge.
